content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"All four blind responses converge on the same primary identification: the 'wise' person is one who fears the LORD and hears and obeys God's word — practical, moral-spiritual skill in godly living rather than mere intellect. They add secondary uses: Christ as personified Wisdom, eschatological readiness (wise virgins/servant), ironic/negative worldly wisdom, and the Magi.","book_summary":"The book defines the wise as 'One who hears God's word and does it, who fears the LORD,' with the fool as the explicit opposite, citing Matt 7:24 (wise builder who hears and does) and Ps 111:10 (fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom).","consensus_core_identification":"The wise = one who fears the LORD and hears/obeys God's word, expressing wisdom in righteous living (contrasted with the fool).","book_core_identification":"The wise = one who hears God's word and does it, who fears the LORD (opposite: fool).","core_relation":"EQUIVALENT","extension_relation":"SAME_CASES","boundary_disagreement":"None. The book omits the consensus's secondary senses (Christological Wisdom, ironic worldly wisdom, the Magi), but omission of alternatives in a terse glossary entry is not a boundary dispute; the central referent and its defining conditions are identical.","material_contradiction":"None. Both identify the wise by the same two marks: fear of the LORD and hearing-plus-doing God's word, with the fool as the antithesis — exactly the consensus contrast noted in Response B and others.","rationale":"The book's definition is a near-verbatim distillation of the consensus primary meaning. Every response leads with the fear-of-the-LORD and hear-and-do formulations (Prov 1:7; 9:10; Ps 111:10; Matt 7:24-27), and the book cites two of those very passages. The wise/fool opposition is also explicitly present in consensus (Response B's notes; Response C's contrast with the foolish). Differences are only in brevity and the absence of secondary/ironic senses, which is immaterial detail rather than disagreement.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue the book narrows 'wise' by reducing it to only the obedience/fear sense, silently excluding the negative 'wise in one's own eyes' usage and other senses the consensus lists — potentially a REFINED narrowing. But those are listed alternatives, not the consensus core, and a glossary defining the positive symbolic sense does not thereby deny the ironic usage.","confidence":"high"}
